source.title: Mathematics Part I
source.edition: Textbook for Class XII Part I, Reprint 2026-27

chapter.name: Application of Derivatives
chapter.blurb: Applications of the derivative: as the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another (including related rates through the Chain Rule and marginal cost and revenue), to find intervals on which a function is increasing or decreasing, and to locate turning points where a function has local maxima or minima. The chapter closes with the absolute maximum and minimum values of a function on a closed interval and applied optimisation problems.

scope_in.item: Interpret dy/dx (or f'(x)) as the rate of change of y with respect to x, evaluate it at x = x0, and read its sign (positive: y increases as x increases; negative: y decreases)
Find the rate of change of area, volume, surface area or circumference with respect to a length (circle, sphere, cube) at a given value
Find marginal cost dC/dx and marginal revenue dR/dx for polynomial cost and revenue functions at a given output

Use the Chain Rule dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt) and dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) to solve related-rate problems with time: ripples, cubes, spheres and balloons, rectangles, a sliding ladder, a sand or water cone, a lamp-post shadow, a point moving on a curve
State the definitions of increasing, decreasing, strictly increasing, strictly decreasing and constant functions on an interval, and of increasing/decreasing at a point

Use Theorem 1 (sign of f'(x) on (a, b) decides increasing, decreasing or constant on [a, b]) to show a function is increasing or decreasing on R or on an interval, including e^x, log x, sin x, cos x and cubics with f'(x) written as a sum of squares

Find the intervals of increase and decrease by solving f'(x) = 0, dividing the domain into disjoint intervals and testing the sign of f'(x) in each, for polynomial and trigonometric functions on restricted intervals
Define maximum, minimum and extreme values of a function on an interval and decide from the function (x^2, |x|, x on (0, 1)) whether they exist
Define points of local maxima and local minima and critical points (f'(c) = 0 or f not differentiable), and know that f'(c) = 0 does not guarantee an extremum (x^3 at 0)
Apply the First Derivative Test (sign change of f'(x) through a critical point), including points of inflexion where f' does not change sign and non-differentiable points such as |x|
Apply the Second Derivative Test (f'(c) = 0 with f''(c) < 0 or > 0) and recognise when it fails (f''(c) = 0 or f not twice differentiable) and revert to the first derivative test

Solve optimisation problems by writing the quantity as a function of one variable and rejecting impossible values: numbers with a given sum, open boxes from sheets, wire cut into a square and circle, profit functions, distances from a point to a curve, cylinders and cones
Distinguish absolute (global) maximum and minimum values from local ones and use Theorems 5 and 6 on a closed interval
Use the four-step working rule (critical points, end points, evaluate, compare) to find absolute maximum and minimum values on a closed interval, including points where f is not differentiable

scope_out.item: Tangents and normals to a curve (slope of a tangent, equations of tangent and normal)
scope_out.reason: Listed in the 6.1 Introduction (p. 147) but there is no tangents-and-normals section in this rationalised Reprint 2026-27 edition: the chapter runs 6.2 Rate of Change, 6.3 Increasing and Decreasing Functions, 6.4 Maxima and Minima and the Summary only

scope_out.item: Approximations and differentials (dy = f'(x) dx, approximate values such as sqrt(25.3))
scope_out.reason: Also promised in the Introduction (p. 147) but no approximations section exists in this edition; the word 'approximate' appears only in Example 35 (p. 181), which is still a rate-of-change computation

scope_out.item: Rolle's Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem as topics in their own right
scope_out.reason: The proof of Theorem 1 cites the Mean Value Theorem (p. 154) but this chapter does not teach or test it, and Chapter 5 of this edition has no MVT section either

scope_out.item: Concavity, using f''(x) to find intervals of concave up/down, and finding points of inflexion by solving f''(x) = 0
scope_out.reason: The book defines a point of inflexion only as a critical point where f'(x) does not change sign (pp. 164, 166); f'' is used solely in the second derivative test
Graphs are used only as illustrations (Figs 6.1-6.19); no curve-tracing procedure is taught

scope_out.item: Proofs of Theorem 2, Theorem 5 (extreme value theorem) and Theorem 6
scope_out.reason: Stated without proof (pp. 164, 172); the result that every continuous function on a closed interval has a maximum and minimum is explicitly 'beyond the scope of the present text' (p. 162)

scope_out.item: Functions of two or more variables, partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers
scope_out.reason: Every optimisation problem in the chapter is reduced to one variable using the given condition

scope_out.item: Newton's method, error estimates and percentage error
scope_out.reason: Not in the chapter; percentage error belongs to the approximations section that this edition does not contain

scope_out.item: Velocity and acceleration as a separate kinematics topic (second derivative of displacement)
scope_out.reason: Only Example 30 (p. 177) uses v = dx/dt to find when a car stops; acceleration is not discussed

concepts.name: Rate of change of a quantity, marginal cost and marginal revenue
concepts.description: Reading dy/dx as the rate of change of y with respect to x, evaluating it at a point, interpreting its sign, and finding marginal cost dC/dx and marginal revenue dR/dx.
concepts.idea: When y depends on x, dy/dx tells how fast y changes as x changes; its value at x = x0 is the rate at that particular x.
concepts.rule: Rate of change of y with respect to x at x = x0 is dy/dx evaluated at x0. A positive rate means y increases as x increases, a negative rate means y decreases. Marginal cost = dC/dx and marginal revenue = dR/dx.
concepts.example: A = pi r^2 gives dA/dr = 2 pi r, so at r = 5 cm the area changes at 10 pi (cm^2 per cm of radius). For R(x) = 3x^2 + 36x + 5, MR = 6x + 36 = 66 at x = 5.

concepts.name: Related rates with respect to time using the Chain Rule
concepts.description: Linking the rates of change of quantities that vary with time through a formula connecting them: circles, cubes, spheres, rectangles, ladders, cones and shadows.
concepts.idea: When quantities change with time and are tied together by a formula, differentiating that formula with respect to t ties their rates together.
concepts.rule: If y = f(x) and x varies with t, then dy/dt = f'(x) . dx/dt. If x = f(t) and y = g(t), dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) when dx/dt != 0. A quantity that is decreasing has a negative rate.
concepts.example: Ripples spread at dr/dt = 4 cm/s. A = pi r^2 gives dA/dt = 2 pi r (dr/dt) = 2 pi (10)(4) = 80 pi cm^2/s when r = 10 cm.

questions.q: If x = f(t) and y = g(t), then by the Chain Rule the rate of change of y with respect to x is
questions.a: (dy/dt) / (dx/dt), provided dx/dt != 0

questions.a: It is wrong. 4 pi r^2 is dV/dr, not dV/dt. By the Chain Rule dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 (dr/dt), so at r = 10 cm, dV/dt = 400 pi (dr/dt), which depends on how fast r grows.
s: Identifies the missing chain factor dr/dt

questions.a: For example: the side x of a square increases at 2 cm/s; how fast is the area increasing when x = 5 cm and when x = 10 cm? A = x^2, so dA/dt = 2x (dx/dt) = 4x. At x = 5 cm it is 20 cm^2/s and at x = 10 cm it is 40 cm^2/s, so the rate grows with the side.
s: Frames a clear question with a constant rate for the side
Uses dA/dt = 2x (dx/dt)
Computes the rate at two side lengths and shows it depends on x

concepts.name: Increasing and decreasing functions and the derivative test
concepts.description: Definitions of increasing, decreasing, strictly increasing, strictly decreasing and constant functions on an interval, and Theorem 1: the sign of f'(x) on (a, b) decides whether f is increasing, decreasing or constant on [a, b].
concepts.idea: Moving left to right, an increasing function's graph never goes down and a decreasing one's never goes up; the sign of the slope f'(x) tells which.
concepts.rule: If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b): f'(x) > 0 for each x in (a, b) gives f increasing on [a, b]; f'(x) < 0 gives f decreasing; f'(x) = 0 gives f constant.
concepts.example: f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x has f'(x) = 3(x - 1)^2 + 1 > 0 for every x, so f is increasing on R.

If f is continuous on [a, b] and f'(x) = 0 for each x in (a, b), then f is a ____ function on [a, b].

questions.a: f'(x) = 2x - 1. For x in (-1, 1/2), f'(x) < 0, so f is decreasing there; for x in (1/2, 1), f'(x) > 0, so f is increasing there. Since f decreases on one part of (-1, 1) and increases on another, it is neither increasing nor decreasing on (-1, 1).

s: Evaluates f'(3 pi/2) = 1 > 0, finding the sign error
Concludes cos x is increasing near 3 pi/2

questions.q: Construct a polynomial function f that is increasing on R but whose derivative is zero at x = 2. Justify your example.
questions.a: For example f(x) = (x - 2)^3. Then f'(x) = 3(x - 2)^2, which is 0 at x = 2 and positive everywhere else. Also if x1 < x2 then x1 - 2 < x2 - 2, so (x1 - 2)^3 < (x2 - 2)^3, i.e. f(x1) < f(x2). Hence f is increasing on R although f'(2) = 0.
s: Gives a suitable polynomial such as (x - 2)^3
Shows f'(2) = 0
Justifies that f is increasing on R

concepts.name: Finding intervals of increase and decrease
concepts.description: Solving f'(x) = 0 to split the domain into disjoint intervals and testing the sign of f'(x) on each to find where a polynomial or trigonometric function is increasing or decreasing.
concepts.idea: The points where f'(x) = 0 cut the line into pieces; on each piece f' keeps one sign, so f either rises or falls throughout that piece.
concepts.rule: Find f'(x), solve f'(x) = 0, divide the domain at those points, and check the sign of f'(x) in each interval: f'(x) > 0 means increasing, f'(x) < 0 means decreasing.
concepts.example: f(x) = 4x^3 - 6x^2 - 72x + 30 gives f'(x) = 12(x - 3)(x + 2); f is increasing on (-infinity, -2) and (3, infinity) and decreasing on (-2, 3).

questions.q: Find the intervals in which f(x) = x^2 + 2x - 5 is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.
questions.a: f'(x) = 2x + 2, which is 0 at x = -1. f'(x) < 0 for x < -1 and f'(x) > 0 for x > -1. So f is strictly decreasing on (-infinity, -1) and strictly increasing on (-1, infinity).

concepts.name: Second derivative test and optimisation problems
concepts.description: Using f'(c) = 0 together with the sign of f''(c) to classify local maxima and minima, recognising when the test fails, and solving word problems (numbers, boxes, profit, mensuration) by maximising or minimising a function of one variable.
concepts.idea: At a stationary point, a graph that bends downward (f'' < 0) is at a hilltop and one that bends upward (f'' > 0) is at a valley bottom; a word problem is solved by turning the quantity into a function of one variable.
concepts.rule: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0, c is a point of local maxima; if f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, local minima; if f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) = 0 the test fails and the first derivative test is used. In word problems, use the given condition to write the quantity in one variable, reject values that are physically impossible, then apply the test.
concepts.example: Two positive numbers with sum 15: S(x) = x^2 + (15 - x)^2, S'(x) = 4x - 30 = 0 gives x = 15/2 and S'' = 4 > 0, so the sum of squares is least when both numbers are 15/2.

concepts.name: Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval
concepts.description: Absolute (global) maximum and minimum values of a continuous function on a closed interval, how they differ from local extrema, and the four-step working rule using critical points and end points.
concepts.idea: On a closed interval, a continuous function always reaches a greatest and a least value, either at a critical point inside or at an end point.
concepts.rule: Working rule: (1) find the critical points of f in [a, b]; (2) take the end points a and b; (3) evaluate f at all these points; (4) the largest value is the absolute maximum and the smallest is the absolute minimum.
concepts.example: f(x) = 2x^3 - 15x^2 + 36x + 1 on [1, 5]: f(1) = 24, f(2) = 29, f(3) = 28, f(5) = 56, so the absolute maximum is 56 at x = 5 and the absolute minimum is 24 at x = 1.

questions.a: For example f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x on [0, 5]. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3). f'(x) changes from positive to negative at x = 1, so x = 1 is a point of local maxima with f(1) = 4. Checking f(0) = 0, f(1) = 4, f(3) = 0 and f(5) = 20, the absolute maximum is 20 at the end point x = 5.
s: Gives a suitable function and closed interval
Shows an interior point of local maxima using f'(x)
Evaluates f at the critical points and end points to show the absolute maximum is at an end point
